questions.stem: What is the difference between income and wealth?
options: Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock of assets held at a point in time
Income is a stock; wealth is a flow
Income includes benefits; wealth does not
They are the same thing measured differently
questions.why: Wealth generates income, and income allows saving which accumulates wealth, so the two reinforce each other.
whyNot: The definitions are the other way round.
Both can be defined to include various components; the distinction is flow against stock.
They are distinct concepts.

questions.stem: Which is always more unequally distributed?
options: Wealth, because it accumulates over a lifetime and is inherited
Income, because wages vary widely
They are equally unequal in every country
It varies unpredictably between countries
questions.why: Many households have little or no wealth at all, whereas almost everyone has some income.
whyNot: Income is more evenly distributed than wealth everywhere.
Wealth is more concentrated in every country.
The pattern is consistent.

questions.stem: What does the Lorenz curve plot?
options: Cumulative percentage of income against cumulative percentage of population, from poorest to richest
Income against the price level
Population against the unemployment rate
The Gini coefficient against time
questions.why: The further the curve bows away from the diagonal line of perfect equality, the greater the inequality.
whyNot: That is unrelated to inequality measurement.
That is a labour market relationship.
The Gini is derived from the curve, not plotted against time on it.

questions.stem: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 represent?
options: Perfect equality
Perfect inequality
Average inequality
An error in the data
questions.why: A coefficient of 1 means one person has everything. Higher means more unequal.
whyNot: That is a coefficient of 1.
There is no fixed average value.
Zero is a valid theoretical value.

questions.stem: How is the Gini coefficient calculated from a Lorenz curve?
options: The area between the curve and the line of equality, divided by the whole area beneath that line
The area under the Lorenz curve divided by the area under the line of equality
The vertical distance between the curve and the line at the midpoint
The slope of the Lorenz curve at its steepest point
questions.why: So a curve lying close to the diagonal gives a small coefficient and a curve bowing far below it gives a large one.
whyNot: That would give the complement of the coefficient.
A single distance does not capture the whole distribution.
The slope at one point is not the measure.

questions.stem: Why can two very different distributions share the same Gini coefficient?
options: It is a single number, so extreme wealth at the top and extreme poverty at the bottom can produce the same value
The coefficient is always inaccurate
The coefficient ignores the size of the population
The coefficient measures wealth rather than income
questions.why: The policy responses to those two situations are completely different, which is why the summary statistic needs supplementing.
whyNot: It is calculated accurately from the data available.
It is a proportional measure, so population size does not distort it.
It is usually measured on income.

questions.stem: Why does the Gini coefficient understate overall inequality?
options: It is usually measured on income rather than wealth, and wealth is far more unequal
It excludes the poorest households from the calculation
It is measured before the population is fully counted
It includes benefits in kind
questions.why: It also ignores benefits in kind such as free health care and education, which reduce effective inequality.
whyNot: All households are included.
Population coverage is not the issue.
It excludes benefits in kind, which works in the other direction.

questions.stem: Why should you always check whether a Gini coefficient is before or after taxes and benefits?
options: The two figures differ substantially, and the difference is the effect of redistribution
Only the pre-tax figure is ever published
The post-tax figure always shows more inequality
The distinction makes no difference to the value
questions.why: Quoting the wrong one can reverse the conclusion about how redistributive a country's system is.
whyNot: Both are published for many countries.
Redistribution normally reduces measured inequality.
The difference is often large.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of inequality within a country?
options: Ownership of capital, since returns accrue to those who already have wealth
The size of the country's population
Membership of the WTO
The number of languages spoken
questions.why: Wage differentials, unequal education, unemployment, the tax and benefit system, inheritance and discrimination are the other main causes.
whyNot: Population size does not determine distribution.
Trade membership is not a direct cause.
Language diversity is not an economic cause.

questions.stem: How does inequality affect enterprise, according to the two-sided argument?
options: Large rewards encourage risk-taking, and where most people have no access to credit, enterprise is suppressed
Inequality always encourages enterprise
Inequality always suppresses enterprise
Inequality has no effect on enterprise
questions.why: Which effect dominates depends on whether the financial system reaches ordinary households, which is the microfinance argument.
whyNot: Lack of access to capital prevents most potential entrepreneurs from starting.
The prospect of reward does encourage risk-taking.
Both effects are substantial.

questions.stem: How does inequality affect savings, and what is the counter-argument?
options: Higher earners save more so aggregate saving rises, and the savings may go abroad while consumption falls
Inequality always reduces aggregate saving
Inequality has no effect on saving
Savings and inequality are unrelated concepts
questions.why: It may raise the funds available and reduce the demand that makes investment worthwhile, and capital flight can remove the savings entirely.
whyNot: Higher-income households save a larger proportion of income.
Marginal propensities to save differ by income level.
The savings ratio depends directly on the distribution.

questions.stem: Why is unequal access to education described as inefficient as well as unjust?
options: The economy loses the productivity of people who would have been highly capable
It raises the cost of providing education
It reduces the number of schools required
It has no effect on productivity
questions.why: Talent is wasted, and unequal education perpetuates inequality into the next generation.
whyNot: Cost is not the efficiency argument.
Fewer schools is not an efficiency gain in this sense.
Human capital is a direct determinant of productivity.

questions.stem: What does the Kuznets hypothesis propose?
options: Inequality first rises and then falls as an economy develops
Inequality falls continuously as an economy develops
Inequality rises continuously with development
Inequality is unrelated to the level of development
questions.why: The evidence is mixed, and several developed economies have seen inequality rise again, so it is a possible pattern rather than a law.
whyNot: The hypothesis describes an inverted U.
The hypothesis predicts a later fall.
The hypothesis links the two explicitly.

questions.stem: What is the strongest framing for an essay on whether inequality should be reduced?
options: Some inequality is necessary for incentives, so the question is how much and whether it reflects contribution
All inequality is unjust and should be eliminated
Inequality is always efficient and should not be reduced
Inequality cannot be measured, so no judgement is possible
questions.why: Market outcomes depend on an initial distribution of assets that is largely inherited, so the source of the inequality matters as much as its extent.
whyNot: Complete equality removes incentives and is not a serious economic position.
Beyond some point inequality becomes self-reinforcing rather than rewarding contribution.
The Gini coefficient and Lorenz curve measure it.

questions.stem: How does inequality affect life expectancy?
options: Lower incomes mean worse nutrition, housing and health care access, so life expectancy is lower among the poorest
Life expectancy is unaffected by income
More unequal societies always have higher average life expectancy
Life expectancy depends only on genetics
questions.why: More unequal societies tend to show worse average health outcomes than more equal ones at the same average income.
whyNot: The relationship is well established.
The evidence points the other way.
Nutrition, sanitation and health care access are major determinants.

questions.stem: How can low interest rates reduce income inequality while raising wealth inequality?
options: They support employment, which helps the poorest, and raise asset prices, which benefits existing wealth owners
They raise wages and lower asset prices
They have no effect on either measure
They reduce both measures simultaneously
questions.why: This applies directly to the post-2008 period and is a genuinely sophisticated point.
whyNot: Low rates tend to raise asset prices.
Both channels are substantial.
The two effects move in opposite directions.
